extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and Office personnel (also useful to patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness during patent examination, covering use of the "obvious to try" rationale, when known work in one field supports adaptation, the role of teaching/suggestion/motivation, common sense, and related Graham factual findings. Focused on factual and legal findings examiners must articulate to support or rebut obviousness conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try rationale (KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp; the fact that a combination was obvious to try might show that it was obvious under §103 (KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the KSR formulation: “When there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp. … the fact that a combination was obvious to try might show that it was obvious under §103.” Use this rationale only where the appropriate factual findings (Graham inquiries) support it; see examples (Alza, Kubin, Perfect Web, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations where ‘obvious to try’ is improperly equated with obviousness (Kubin’s two classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two classes of situations where equating ‘obvious to try’ with obviousness is erroneous: (1) when ‘obvious to try’ would require varying all parameters or trying each of numerous possible choices until one possibly arrived at a successful result, where the prior art gave either no indication of which parameters were critical or no direction as to which of many possible choices is likely to be successful; and (2) when ‘obvious to try’ was to explore a new technology or general approach that seemed promising, where the prior art gave only general guidance as to the particular form of the claimed invention or how to achieve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Kubin: these classes limit application of obvious-to-try. If a case fits either class, obvious-to-try reasoning is not appropriate. Examples: broad unexplored fields, numerous unconstrained parameters, or prior art providing only general guidance (not specific, finite options).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required to invoke an obvious-to-try rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on an obvious-to-try rationale, there must generally be (a) a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, and (b) a reasonable expectation of success that one of those solutions would work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should make Graham factual findings and articulate why the prior art would have led the skilled artisan to try the limited set of options with a reasonable expectation of success. Examples: Alza (finite methods + reasonable expectation), Perfect Web (finite, predictable solutions + no unexpected results). By contrast, Takeda, Ortho‑McNeil, and Sanofi demonstrate where these elements are absent and obvious-to-try fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/meaning of ‘finite’ in context (Ortho‑McNeil)
rubrics_metrics.description: When KSR speaks of a ‘finite’ number of options, ‘finite’ means ‘small or easily traversed’ in the context of the art in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the ‘finite’ requirement with reference to the state of the art: a large universe of options may still be treated as narrowed if the prior art funnels the skilled artisan to a reduced, easily traversed set. Ortho‑McNeil emphasizes context — what is ‘finite’ depends on the art and its customary practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success (predictability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable expectation of success is required for an obviousness rejection based on obvious-to-try or combinations; the claimed outcome must have been reasonably predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kubin (where conventional methods would have made obtaining the claimed nucleic acid reasonably predictable), Bayer (prior art funneled formulator to two practical options producing predictable results), but Sanofi and Ortho‑McNeil show unpredictability/unexpected therapeutic advantage can negate a reasonable expectation. Lack of absolute predictability does not defeat reasonable expectation if success was reasonably predictable from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results / unexpected properties can overcome prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results or properties (e.g., surprising therapeutic advantages, lack of toxicity, serendipitous discovery) can rebut or overcome a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Takeda (unexpected lack of toxicity for pioglitazone); Sanofi (absolute stereoselectivity of the D-isomer provided unexpected therapeutic advantage); Ortho‑McNeil (serendipitous discovery of anticonvulsant properties). Examiners must consider such evidence and may not sustain an obviousness rejection if unexpected results are persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large number of options does not automatically mean nonobvious; consider reduced option set guided by prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a large number of options does not in and of itself lead to a conclusion of nonobviousness. Where prior art teachings lead one of ordinary skill to a narrower set of options, that reduced set is the appropriate one to consider for an obvious-to-try analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bayer example: although many TZD compounds were known, the prior art funneled the formulator toward two options (normal pill or enteric‑coated pill); thus, the reduced set governs the obvious-to-try inquiry. Examiners should identify how prior art narrows choices before concluding nonobviousness based on quantity of options alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of common sense in obviousness determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense may inform the analysis of obviousness, but must be explained with sufficient reasoning and supported by the evidence of record; it cannot be an unexplained, conclusory invocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect Web and other cases: common sense has long been recognized to inform obviousness when accompanied by reasoned analysis. Cite precedents (In re Bozek, In re Zurko, DyStar, In re Kahn, B/E Aerospace). Arendi warns against invoking common sense without reasoned, evidentiary support. Examiners must provide a reasoned explanation that avoids conclusory generalizations if relying on common sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable adaptation to same or different field — five required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on the rationale that known work in one field would prompt a predictable variation for use in the same or different field, Office personnel must articulate: (1) that the prior art included a similar or analogous device (method, or product); (2) that design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; (3) that the differences between claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or a known principle; (4) that one of ordinary skill could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham factual findings necessary for the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale is that design incentives/market forces could have prompted predictable variation. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion. Examples: Dann, Leapfrog, KSR, Catan illustrate application of these findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM) rationale — required articulations
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on a teaching, suggestion, or motivation to modify or combine prior art references, Office personnel must: (1) resolve the Graham factual inquiries; (2) find some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (in references or general knowledge) to modify/combine; (3) find a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) make any other Graham findings necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale is that a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art to achieve the claimed invention and would have had a reasonable expectation of success. If any of these findings cannot be made (e.g., no motivation, no expectation), the TSM rationale cannot be used. Cited authorities: DyStar, In re Kahn, In re Lee (earlier TSM discussion) and later KSR-modified approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a reason to select a particular lead compound or starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection based on starting from or modifying a prior art lead compound requires a reason to select that compound as a lead; absent such a reason, the modification path may not be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takeda and Ortho‑McNeil illustrate that if the closest prior art compound had known disadvantages that would teach away from using it as a lead, or there was no reason a skilled artisan would have chosen the particular starting compound/pathway, a prima facie obviousness case may fail. Examiners should identify and articulate why a skilled artisan would have selected the specific lead compound or path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine application of conventional methods to a known product can support obviousness when success was predictable
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art discloses a product (e.g., a polypeptide) and conventional, routine methods in the art (e.g., sequencing, isolation techniques) would have allowed obtaining the claimed product, a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation that the claimed product could be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kubin example: Valiante disclosed the polypeptide and Sambrook disclosed conventional methods for sequencing/isolating the nucleic acid; the Board found a reasonable expectation of successfully obtaining the claimed nucleic acid. Examiners should articulate the specific conventional methods and why they would have produced the claimed invention with reasonable predictability.
